pool.prompt: A new attacher files an OTMR application on a Monday. Per 47 CFR 1.1411, when does the 15-day approval clock for simple make-ready START?
choices: The same Monday the application is filed
On the date the pole owner declares the application COMPLETE — an incomplete application does not start the clock, similar to the Section 106 completeness-triggered clock covered in T09
Exactly 30 days after filing, regardless of completeness
The clock never has a defined start date under OTMR rules
pool.explanation: Like several other regulatory review clocks covered across this training (Section 106's 30-day SHPO clock, the FCC's municipal shot clocks), the OTMR simple make-ready clock is tied to application COMPLETENESS, not the raw filing date — an incomplete submission does not start the 15-day clock.
pool.citation: 47 CFR 1.1411 — reused from the T01 research pass's independent verification of the OTMR framework.

pool.prompt: Classify each make-ready scenario as Simple (OTMR eligible) or Complex (multi-party required).

items.label: Raising a coax cable 4 inches using existing hooks, no splicing needed
A telephone cable must be spliced because all its slack is deployed

pool.explanation: Simple make-ready (OTMR-eligible) covers work like repositioning an existing attachment using its existing hardware with no splicing — a single qualified contractor can complete it in one visit. Complex make-ready — like a splice required because a cable has no remaining slack — typically requires the involvement of the affected attacher and falls outside the streamlined OTMR single-visit process.

pool.prompt: If a pole owner declares OTMR make-ready 'complex' on 5 poles in an application, what must they provide per 47 CFR 1.1411?
choices: Nothing — the pole owner has sole, unreviewable discretion to classify make-ready as complex with no justification required

A reasoned explanation/basis for the complex classification — the pole owner cannot simply assert complexity without justification, since an unreviewable blanket complex-classification power would undermine OTMR's purpose of streamlining make-ready for genuinely simple work
A cash payment to the new attacher for the inconvenience
Nothing is required until the new attacher formally appeals the classification
pool.explanation: OTMR's framework requires the pole owner to provide a basis for a complex-make-ready classification rather than exercising unreviewable discretion — this check exists specifically because an unconstrained ability to declare any make-ready 'complex' would defeat the purpose of the streamlined simple-make-ready pathway.
pool.citation: 47 CFR 1.1411 — reused from the T01 research pass.

pool.prompt: Per 47 CFR 1.1411, if the pole owner does not respond to a complete OTMR application within 15 calendar days of the completeness declaration, what happens?
choices: The application is automatically denied

The application is treated as deemed approved — the 15-calendar-day figure functions as a hard deadline with a specific consequence (deemed approval) for non-response, not merely an aspirational target
The applicant must resubmit the entire application from scratch
The clock simply resets and restarts for another 15 days indefinitely
pool.explanation: The deemed-approved consequence is what gives the 15-day figure real teeth as a deadline — without a specific consequence for non-response, a stated timeline would be aspirational rather than enforceable; the deemed-approved mechanism is what makes OTMR's speed guarantee meaningful in practice.

pool.prompt: What was the specific FCC action that created the modern OTMR (One-Touch Make-Ready) framework?
choices: The Telecommunications Act of 1996

The FCC's 2018 pole attachment/infrastructure order (the same broader 2018 rulemaking that also established the municipal small-wireless-facility shot clocks covered in T09) — OTMR streamlined simple make-ready into a single-visit process for a qualified contractor hired by the new attacher
The original 1996 Pole Attachment Act
A 2023 FCC order responding to the Sackett v. EPA decision
pool.explanation: OTMR emerged from the FCC's 2018 infrastructure-deployment rulemaking (the same broader order package that established the municipal shot clocks covered in T09.L08) — allowing a qualified contractor hired by the new attacher to perform simple make-ready in a single visit, rather than waiting for each existing attachment owner to separately schedule their own work.

pool.prompt: Why does the simple-vs-complex make-ready classification matter so much to a project's schedule, beyond just determining who performs the physical work?
choices: It has no schedule impact — simple and complex make-ready always take the same amount of time

Simple (OTMR-eligible) make-ready follows a single-visit, streamlined timeline with a deemed-approved backstop, while complex make-ready typically requires coordination with the affected attacher's own schedule and resources — a route with a high proportion of complex make-ready can face a substantially longer and less predictable timeline than one that's mostly OTMR-eligible
The classification only affects cost, never schedule
Complex make-ready is always faster than simple make-ready because it involves more parties working in parallel
pool.explanation: The practical schedule consequence of the simple/complex distinction is real: OTMR-eligible work has a defined, backstopped fast timeline, while complex make-ready depends on the affected attacher's own scheduling and resource availability — a project team assessing a route's overall timeline needs to know the actual mix of simple vs. complex make-ready across the poles involved, not just the total pole count.

pool.prompt: A route has 20 poles requiring make-ready: 15 are simple (OTMR-eligible, no splicing) and 5 are complex (require an existing attacher's coordination). What is the correct project-management approach to minimize total schedule time?
choices: Wait until all 5 complex poles are fully resolved before starting any of the 15 simple poles, to keep the project sequential and easy to track

Run the OTMR-eligible simple make-ready and the complex make-ready processes in PARALLEL from the start — since the two tracks have different timelines and different responsible parties, sequencing them one-after-another needlessly extends the total project schedule compared to working both tracks simultaneously
Cancel the 5 complex poles from the route entirely to avoid the coordination requirement
Convert the 5 complex poles to simple poles by re-classifying them without pole-owner involvement
pool.explanation: Because OTMR-eligible and complex make-ready involve different processes, timelines, and responsible parties, running them in parallel from the start — rather than sequencing simple-then-complex or complex-then-simple — minimizes the project's total schedule time, since the two tracks don't have to wait on each other to begin.

pool.prompt: Why does OTMR's deemed-approved mechanism specifically require the application to be COMPLETE before the 15-day clock starts, rather than starting the clock on any submission regardless of completeness?
choices: It doesn't actually matter — the clock always starts on the raw filing date regardless of completeness

Starting the clock only on a complete application protects the pole owner from being forced into a deemed-approval outcome based on insufficient information to actually evaluate the request — the completeness requirement balances the new attacher's interest in a fast, predictable timeline against the pole owner's need for adequate information to make a real safety/engineering determination
The completeness requirement exists purely to slow down new attachers and has no legitimate engineering purpose
Completeness only matters for complex make-ready, never for simple make-ready
pool.explanation: The completeness trigger reflects a deliberate balance: it protects the deemed-approved mechanism's integrity by ensuring the pole owner actually had adequate information to evaluate the request before the clock (and its automatic-approval consequence) starts running — without this safeguard, a pole owner could be forced into deemed approval of a request they never had a fair opportunity to properly review.
